meta.title: Who originally recorded "Twist and Shout"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a Beatles original. "Twist and Shout" was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns and first recorded in 1961 by The Top Notes on Atlantic — a flop. The Isley Brothers made it a hit in 1962; the Beatles' 1963 version is a cover.
meta.ogDescription: Everyone thinks it’s a Beatles song. It was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns, first cut by The Top Notes in 1961, and made famous by the Isley Brothers in 1962. The Beatles came third.

answer.label: Not a Beatles original — a 1961 Top Notes single
answer.sourceLine: Almost everyone takes ‘Twist and Shout’ for a Beatles original, but the Beatles’ 1963 version is a cover — and not even the first cover. The song was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns and first recorded in 1961 by The Top Notes on Atlantic Records, produced by a young Phil Spector. That version flopped. The Isley Brothers turned it into a hit in 1962, and the Beatles arrived third, in 1963.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Atlantic Records

original.charted: Did not chart — the single was not a hit
original.cover: The Beatles — recorded 11 February 1963 at EMI Studios, London, and released on Please Please Me. Issued as a US single in 1964, it reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became the version most listeners now treat as definitive.

docMeta.dd: 1961 (Atlantic) — produced by Phil Spector, did not chart

trail: The song was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns and first recorded on 23 February 1961 by The Top Notes for Atlantic Records, in a session produced by Phil Spector. The single failed to chart Wikipedia ↗.

The Isley Brothers re-recorded it in 1962 for Wand Records, adding the now-iconic bridge — the ascending build and the whooping call-and-response — and took it to No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100, their first Top 20 hit. This is the version that made the song famous.

The Beatles recorded their cover on 11 February 1963 for Please Please Me, modelled closely on the Isley Brothers’ arrangement. It became so beloved that most listeners now assume the song began with them — two recordings and two years too late the history ↗.

externalLinks.label: The Top Notes
externalLinks.what: The original recording artist — an American R&B vocal group who cut the song first, in 1961, before it was a hit for anyone.

externalLinks.label: Bert Berns
externalLinks.what: Co-writer of the song — the songwriter and producer behind ‘Twist and Shout’, ‘Piece of My Heart’, and ‘Brown Eyed Girl’.

authors.name: The Top Notes
authors.heading: About The Top Notes
authors.bio: The Top Notes were an American R&B and doo-wop group centred on singers Derek Martin and Howard Guyton. In February 1961 they made the very first recording of ‘Twist and Shout’ for Atlantic Records, produced by a then-unknown Phil Spector — and it flopped. It is a strange footnote of pop history that the group who introduced one of its most-covered songs are the one act almost nobody remembers.

authors.name: The Isley Brothers
authors.kicker: The version that made it a hit
authors.heading: About The Isley Brothers
authors.bio: The Isley Brothers re-recorded ‘Twist and Shout’ in 1962 for Wand Records and turned a flop into a hit, reaching No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100 — their first Top 20 single. Their arrangement invented the parts everyone now sings: the ascending build in the bridge and the whooping call-and-response. The Beatles’ famous cover follows their blueprint, not the Top Notes’ original, which makes them the hinge of the whole story — and the version the Beatles’ fame quietly buried.

authors.name: The Beatles
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Beatles
authors.bio: The Beatles recorded ‘Twist and Shout’ on 11 February 1963 for Please Please Me, with John Lennon’s raw, throat-shredding vocal taken in a single late-session take. Their version is genuinely theirs and genuinely great; the only error is chronological. It is a cover of a cover — the Isley Brothers made it a hit in 1962, and The Top Notes recorded it first in 1961.

authors.name: Phil Medley & Bert Berns
authors.heading: About the writers
authors.bio: ‘Twist and Shout’ was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns, the latter credited on some pressings under the pseudonym Bert Russell. Berns (1929–1967) was one of the great soul songwriters and producers, also behind ‘Piece of My Heart’ and ‘Brown Eyed Girl’. They are the figures the song’s fame obscures most completely: not the famous band, not the hit-making group, but the two writers whose names ride under every version.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a double misattribution: not only is the Beatles’ record a cover, it is a cover of a cover. The song passed through two other acts before the band the public credits ever touched it.

items.why: The Beatles’ 1963 version is a cover. The song was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns and recorded twice by others first the history ↗.
Cut for Atlantic and produced by Phil Spector, the first version never charted — which is exactly why later covers could eclipse it so completely. There was no famous original standing in the way.
The Isleys added the bridge and the whoops and took the song to No. 17 — the arrangement the Beatles then borrowed. The middle version, and the most influential, is the one most often skipped over.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns, first recorded by The Top Notes in 1961, made a hit by the Isley Brothers in 1962, and made famous — but not originated — by the Beatles in 1963 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: A cover eclipses its original most completely when the original never had its moment. The Top Notes’ 1961 recording sank on release, so there was no hit occupying the public’s memory of the song. That left the field open — first for the Isley Brothers, and then for the Beatles, whose version simply became the version.

The twist is that the recording everyone imitates is not the original at all. The Isley Brothers built the bridge and the call-and-response in 1962, and the Beatles followed their arrangement in 1963. So the ‘Beatles song’ is a cover of the Isleys’ cover of a flop — three acts deep before it reached the band that gets the credit.
detailsBody: Phil Medley and Bert Berns write the song (early 1960s).
The Top Notes record it first, February 1961, for Atlantic; Phil Spector produces; it does not chart.
The Isley Brothers re-record it in 1962 for Wand, add the bridge, and reach US No. 17.
The Beatles record their cover, 11 February 1963, for Please Please Me, following the Isleys’ arrangement.
The Beatles’ version becomes definitive, and both earlier records fade from public memory.
context.pull: The ‘Beatles song’ is a cover of a cover of a flop — three acts deep before the credit lands.
